title: Compound Interest
short: A = P(1 + r/n)ⁿᵗ: interest earns interest.
trouble: Students use the yearly rate for each period without dividing by n.

blocks.html: In Algebra 1 you rewrote a yearly growth rate as a monthly one (Rewriting Exponential Expressions). Banks do exactly that when they compound interest several times a year.

$$A = P\left(1 + \frac{r}{n}\right)^{nt}$$ $P$ is the starting amount, $r$ the yearly rate as a decimal, $n$ the number of compounding periods per year and $t$ the number of years. Each period earns $\frac{r}{n}$, and there are $nt$ periods.

Interest earns interest. If a period's rate is $i$, the balance at the end of the period is the old balance plus $i$ times it, which is the old balance times $(1 + i)$. After $N$ periods you have multiplied by $(1 + i)$ $N$ times: $P(1 + i)^N$. With $n$ periods per year, $i = \frac{r}{n}$ and $N = nt$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: \$1000 at 6% per year. The curve $f$ compounds $n$ times a year; the dashed line $g$ is simple interest (no interest on interest). Raise $n$: the curve rises, but only a little.

blocks.title: Monthly compounding
blocks.q: \$2000 is invested at 4.8% per year, compounded monthly. Find the balance after 5 years.

blocks.title: Comparing frequencies
blocks.q: \$1000 at 6% for 10 years: compare yearly and quarterly compounding.

blocks.html: Using the yearly rate for every period without dividing by $n$. Monthly compounding of 6% is $0.5\%$ per month, not $6\%$ per month. $1000(1.06)^{120}$ would claim over a million dollars after 10 years, which is clearly wrong. Divide the rate by $n$ and multiply the years by $n$.
